faq.a: No direct progression; they are distinct entities, though rare adenomas may harbor mutations that predispose to malignancy.
faq.q: Can an adrenal adenoma become carcinoma?

faq.a: Usually not; imaging and hormone tests suffice. Biopsy is reserved for suspected metastasis when the primary is unknown.
Repeat imaging at 6–12 months; if stable, then every 2–3 years. Hormone tests if the adenoma was functional.
faq.q: What follow‑up is required after removing a benign adenoma?

exam: A 45‑year‑old woman with an incidental 5 cm adrenal mass and suppressed ACTH – what is the next step? — Assess CT washout; if >60% proceed to laparoscopic adrenalectomy.
How does the Weiss score differentiate adenoma from carcinoma? — Scores ≥3 (high mitoses, necrosis, invasion) indicate carcinoma.
Why is ketoconazole used before surgery in cortisol‑producing tumors? — It lowers cortisol, decreasing infection and wound‑healing complications.
What imaging feature most strongly suggests carcinoma? — Heterogeneous enhancement with >10 HU on non‑contrast CT and <60% washout.

A patient with hypertension, hypokalemia, and a 3 cm adrenal mass – which test confirms primary aldosteronism? — Plasma aldosterone/renin ratio; a high ratio (>20) supports aldosterone‑producing adenoma.
When is open adrenalectomy preferred over laparoscopy? — Suspected carcinoma, tumor >6 cm, or evidence of local invasion.
What is the role of mitotane in adrenal carcinoma? — It is an adrenolytic agent used for metastatic disease; monitor for adrenal insufficiency.

How can a pheochromocytoma be distinguished from an adrenal carcinoma clinically? — Pheochromocytoma presents with episodic hypertension, palpitations, and positive plasma metanephrines, whereas carcinoma may have cortisol or androgen excess.
ai.title: Adrenal Adenoma versus Carcinoma
ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Adrenal adenomas are benign, hormonally inactive or mildly functional tumors, while carcinomas are malignant, often hormone‑producing and aggressive. Differentiating them relies on imaging, hormone assays, and pathology, especially where resources are limited.

b: Incidence: adenoma 3–7% of adults on CT; carcinoma 1–2 per million per year
Typical age: adenoma 40–60 y, carcinoma 30–50 y, slight female predominance in carcinoma
sections.p: Adrenal cortical tumors arise from the zona fasciculata/reticularis. Adenomas are common incidentalomas; carcinomas are rare (<0.2% of adrenal masses) but carry high mortality.

b: Key pathways: Wnt/β‑catenin, p53, IGF‑2 overexpression
Hormone excess results from autonomous steroid synthesis
sections.p: Both tumors originate from mutations in adrenal cortical cells affecting steroidogenesis pathways (e.g., CTNNB1, TP53, IGF2). Adenomas often have benign mutations; carcinomas acquire additional oncogenic hits.

b: Loss of feedback inhibition → cortisol, aldosterone, or androgen excess
ACTH levels usually suppressed in cortisol‑producing tumors
sections.p: Normal adrenal cortex is regulated by ACTH and intra‑adrenal autocrine loops. Tumors lose ACTH dependence, producing hormones autonomously.

b: Carcinoma: rapid growth, local invasion, distant spread (lung, liver, bone)
Adenoma: usually stable size; functional types cause Cushing’s, Conn’s, or virilisation
sections.p: Malignant transformation leads to uncontrolled proliferation, invasion, and metastasis. Benign adenomas may enlarge or secrete hormones causing clinical syndromes.

b: Urgent surgery if suspicion of carcinoma or hormone‑life‑threatening excess
Long‑term surveillance for adenomas >4 cm or growing lesions
sections.p: Distinguishing adenoma from carcinoma guides surgery, follow‑up, and oncologic therapy. In low‑resource settings, reliance on clinical clues and basic imaging is essential.
When CT/MRI unavailable, use ultrasound size (>4 cm concerning) and clinical hormone excess to decide surgery.

t.b: Is the lesion benign‑appearing? → <10 HU on non‑contrast and >60% washout suggests adenoma; >10 HU or <60% washout raises carcinoma concern
Does the mass lose signal on out‑of‑phase images? → Signal loss supports adenoma; lack of loss suggests carcinoma

t.a: 24‑hour urinary free cortisol or overnight dexamethasone suppression
t.b: Is cortisol excess present? → Positive test indicates functional tumor; helps prioritize surgery
Is there primary aldosteronism? → Elevated ratio points to aldosterone‑producing adenoma
Is there androgen excess? → Elevated levels suggest functional adenoma or carcinoma
Can cytology help? → Generally avoided due to seeding risk; only if metastasis suspected elsewhere
Is the tumor malignant? → Score ≥3 indicates carcinoma; requires surgical pathology

b: Laparoscopic adrenalectomy for ≤6 cm, non‑invasive adenoma
Open adrenalectomy for suspected carcinoma, tumor >6 cm, or invasion
Mitotane for metastatic carcinoma; avoid if liver failure
Control hormone excess pre‑op: ketoconazole or metyrapone for cortisol; spironolactone for aldosterone
sections.p: Surgery is first‑line for both, but extent differs. Adenomas may be removed laparoscopically; carcinomas often need open adrenalectomy with possible lymphadenectomy.

b: Pheochromocytoma – catecholamine excess, positive plasma metanephrines
Metastatic adrenal lesion – history of lung/breast cancer, bilateral lesions
Myelolipoma – fat‑density on CT, benign
Small carcinomas may have low HU and washout mimicking adenoma
Cortisol suppression tests can be false‑negative in cyclic Cushing’s
Rapidly enlarging mass, severe hypertension, hypokalemia, or uncontrolled cortisol excess
Signs of metastatic disease: bone pain, weight loss, jaundice
